This suggests a neurological, neuromuscular, or structural spinal process. Key differentials include spinal cord compression (e.g., from tumor, stenosis, or myelopathy), peripheral neuropathy, motor neuron disease (e.g., ALS), or inflammatory demyelinating conditions (e.g., chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy or subacute transverse myelitis). To narrow the differential, I must determine the level and pattern of involvement: Is it upper motor neuron (spastic, hyperreflexic, Babinski+) vs. lower motor neuron (flaccid, hyporeflexic, atrophy) vs. sensory ataxia? Presence of sensory symptoms (numbness, tingling, loss of sensation), bowel/bladder dysfunction (suggesting spinal cord or cauda equina involvement), or weakness distribution (proximal vs. distal, symmetric vs. asymmetric) is critical. Bladder/bowel symptoms are particularly urgent red flags for cord compression or conus/cauda equina syndrome.

[QUERY] Have you noticed any changes in bladder control (e.g., urgency, retention, incontinence) or bowel function (e.g., constipation, incontinence)?

It also raises suspicion for conditions like HTLV-1–associated myelopathy (HAM/TSP), vitamin B12 deficiency (subacute combined degeneration), or hereditary spastic paraplegia — though the latter typically spares bladder early on. To further localize and characterize the lesion, I need to assess sensory level (a hallmark of spinal cord pathology), presence of spasticity, and lower limb reflexes. A sensory level — especially if well-defined — would confirm spinal cord involvement and help estimate the anatomical level.
